extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, law students, and practitioners dealing with assignments and title in patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and principles governing assignments, contracts to assign, licenses, joint ownership, and related remedies (reissue/renewal effects) in patent law; how these instruments affect title, notice, warranties, and remedies between parties and as against third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording of assignments as notice for existing patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Recording of assignments of existing patents (e.g., act of 1836, §11 requiring recording within three months) operates as notice to everybody of the title of the assignee and is aimed at protecting subsequent bona fide purchasers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recording a conveyance of an issued patent points to the patent conveyed and allows the public to ascertain what passed by the assignment. This protection applies to patents already issued; the statute contemplates the recording of assignments of existing patents and thereby gives constructive notice to third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording contracts to convey future inventions does not reliably give notice
rubrics_metrics.description: A contract to convey an invention not yet in esse, even if recorded, generally does not operate as notice of title to subsequent purchasers and is 'of no greater force than as the personal covenants of the inventor, to be specifically enforced against him.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a recorded contract for a future invention cannot, by its nature, inform the public what invention was contemplated, subsequent purchasers are not bound to search elsewhere; parties should understand such contracts will not necessarily defeat later titles obtained by the inventor after perfecting the invention and obtaining a patent. Recording such contracts may have practical benefits in some cases, but statutory recording protection is not intended for them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere naked assignment does not import warranty of validity
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere naked assignment of an interest in a patent does not import a warranty by the assignor of the validity of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent words implying an undertaking as to validity, an assignment is to be regarded as a sale of an ascertained chattel (the patent) where both parties have equal opportunity to inform themselves; thus, no implied warranty of validity arises unless express words or equivalent circumstances create one. However, words may be used that do import a warranty, and principles developed under licenses can apply to assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: No implied warranty of title or quality on sale of ascertained patent interest
rubrics_metrics.description: On the sale of a known ascertained article (including an ascertained patent interest), there is generally no implied warranty of title or quality unless there is fraud or an express warranty or equivalent circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (e.g., Parke B. in Morely v. Attenborough) summarize that a vendor is not liable for a bad title without express warranty. Parties with equal means of inquiry (as to novelty, utility, prior use) contract for the patent 'such as it was' and must look to their own judgment unless the contract indicates a promise of indefeasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recitals or clauses may import a warranty of title or validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Words used in an assignment, license, or other instrument (including recitals) may import a warranty extending to the validity of the patent if the language so indicates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The effect of such recitals has most frequently arisen under licenses, but the same principles apply to assignments and contracts to assign: look to the instrument's language to determine whether an implied warranty is created.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment operates as present grant when it vests exclusive right
rubrics_metrics.description: To constitute an assignment there must be a present grant which vests in the grantee the exclusive right to the whole patent, or some undivided part of it, or a whole or undivided part of some territorial interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether an instrument is a present assignment or merely a contract to assign is a question of construction; one element is whether the interest existed in esse at the time (presently existing interest vs. future interest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of part vests undivided interest; creates joint proprietorship
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment of part of a patent constitutes the assignee a joint owner with the assignor, in whom the residue of the interest remains; assignment vests an indefeasible title to the whole or some part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joint ownership results from assignment of an undivided share; the assignee holds an indefeasible interest in the allocated portion of the monopoly granted by the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint proprietors of a patent are not partners by mere ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Joint proprietors (tenants in common) of a patent are not, by the mere fact of joint ownership, to be regarded as partners; partnership relations arise only if they agree to work the patent together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a mere proprietor cannot be compelled to share profits or be prevented from working the patent himself, partnership law does not automatically apply. If they agree to work jointly or the contract fixes profit shares, partnership principles and equitable enforcement may govern accounting and rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights and remedies between co-owners exercising patent privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of partnership or contract creating express accountability, one part owner generally cannot be enjoined by another nor sued in infringement for exercising rights secured by the patent; each co-owner holds an equal right to use and license the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat equitable titles as legal where convertible, and will not interfere to assert superior equity unless a contract modifies tenants-in-common rights. If one co-owner wilfully and systematically acts to deprive another of profits (e.g., by selling at insignificant prices), the proper remedy is a special action on the case alleging special damage and attempted exclusion, not ordinarily an action for infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstances where a part-owner may sue a co-owner for appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: A part owner has been held (in at least one case) to maintain an action of infringement against a co-proprietor and recover a proportionate share of the value of the property appropriated where the co-owner wrongfully appropriates the whole property (analogous to trover).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This view relies on analogy to conversion of chattels: if one owner sells or appropriates the joint property to the injury of another, the injured co-owner may have a tort remedy. But the doctrine is limited and controversial—where the exercise is simply making/using/vending (rights each tenant can exercise), infringement will usually not lie; account or action on the case may be more appropriate depending on facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between reissue and renewal and effect on assignees
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a clear distinction between the operation of assignments upon the reissue of the original patent and upon extension/renewal; reissue (surrender to correct specification) is treated as amending the original patent from its commencement, while renewal/extension adds further term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An assignee holding legal title at time of surrender and reissue should join or consent to surrender; the statute preserves assignees' rights. A patentee cannot affect the rights of an assignee by surrender/reissue without his consent; reissued term enures to the benefit of assignees who held legal title at the time of surrender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue does not vacate prior assignments; assignee's interest continues
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee surrenders and obtains a reissue, previous assignments are not vacated; the reissued term enures to the benefit of the assignee without need of a new assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an assignee has consented to surrender, the reissue enures to his benefit and becomes his act even if he is not of record in the reissue application; he is a proper party in infringement suits within the assigned territory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracts to convey future interests (renewals/extensions) are generally not assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: A contract to convey a future interest in a term not yet obtained (e.g., renewals or extensions not obtained at the time of contract) is generally not an assignment; the future interest being not in esse prevents present vesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have held such instruments operate as personal covenants rather than present grants, though exceptions exist (e.g., Gaylor v. Wilder) which must be examined. An offer to perform a condition precedent does not necessarily convert such a contract into a present grant.
